title: Mastering Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (GAT): Precision & Correction
summary: Goldmann Applanation Tonometry remains the 'gold standard' for IOP measurement, yet it is fraught with systematic errors. This guide details how to identify, troubleshoot, and correct for biomechanical variables, specifically Central Corneal Thickness (CCT).

sections.title: Definition & Principle
sections.content: GAT is based on the Imbert-Fick Law: P = F / A (Pressure = Force / Area). It assumes the cornea is an ideal, thin, dry, elastic sphere with a 3.06mm applanation diameter. At this diameter, the force of surface tension of the tear film and the resistance of the cornea to bending cancel each other out.

sections.title: Troubleshooting Checklist
content: 1. Check calibration of the tonometer head (0, 2, 6 markings).
2. Ensure patient is not holding their breath (Valsalva).
3. Ensure the patient is not squeezing their lids (avoid pressure on the globe).
5. Verify the mires are centered and symmetrical before reading.

sections.title: Red Flags in Tonometry
content: Inaccurate mires in patients with irregular astigmatism (>3.00D).
Readings obtained over an epithelial defect or corneal edema.
Measurements taken immediately post-LASIK/PRK (corneal biomechanics altered).
High IOP readings that do not correlate with optic nerve appearance (C/D ratio).

sections.title: Impact of CCT on Glaucoma Risk
Key Clinical Pearls
content: OHTS Study: Patients with thinner CCT were at higher risk of progressing from Ocular Hypertension to Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma.
Always interpret IOP in the context of CCT; do not rely on GAT as the sole diagnostic factor.
For irregular corneas, consider alternative methods like the Perkins Tonometer or Pascal Dynamic Contour Tonometer.
The mires should represent two concentric circles of equal width.
